title: Trustworthy health-related tweets on social media in Saudi Arabia: Tweet metadata analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis of Arabic health-related tweets from Saudi Arabia (Twitter API, two 7-day windows in 2018). Pairs of medical doctors labelled tweets accurate or inaccurate against their clinical judgement, and the paper reports a share of items judged inaccurate with a denominator: 34 of 109 tweets (31.2%) classified as untrustworthy health information. That is CONTENT, judged against an external ground truth (expert clinician verification of factual accuracy), not a DISCERN/GQS-style quality score.

estimates.date: Two datasets extracted 18 May 2018 and 7 August 2018, each covering the preceding week (Twitter API limit)
estimates.measure_type: % of health-related tweets classified as untrustworthy (inaccurate health information) by two agreeing medical doctors
estimates.denominator: 109 health-related Arabic tweets on which both assigned doctors gave the same accurate/inaccurate label (from 300 labelled, drawn from 552 health-related tweets in a random sample of 2,800 taken from 97,248 lexicon-extracted original tweets)
estimates.definition: Both doctors labelled the tweet 'inaccurate health information'; tweets either doctor marked 'not sure', or on which the two disagreed, were dropped from the denominator
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, tweets are considered to be trustworthy if they are
estimates.source_quote: A total of 34 out of 109 tweets (31.2%) in the dataset used in this study were classified as untrustworthy health information.
estimates.page_loc: Methods, Trustworthiness Classification, p. 6; also Abstract, Results; Figure 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Medical doctors, each tweet independently labelled by two of them as accurate, inaccurate or not sure; disagreements and 'not sure' labels excluded rather than adjudicated, so no agreement statistic is reported for the accuracy coding. The Cohen kappa of .872 in the Methods belongs to the earlier health-relevance filtering by two non-clinical annotators, not to the accuracy labels. The paper says 10 doctors in the Methods but 20 in the Limitations (10 forms of 30 tweets, each sent to two doctors).
estimates.moderator_quote: A health lexicon was used to extract health-related tweets using the Twitter application programming interface and the results were further filtered manually. A total of 300 tweets were each labeled by two medical doctors; the doctors agreed that 109 tweets were either accurate or inaccurate.
estimates.notes: The denominator retains only 109 of the 300 doctor-labelled tweets (36%): every tweet a doctor found ambiguous or on which two doctors disagreed was dropped. The authors flag this themselves ('may have thus excluded a class of health tweets that were not studied'), and the direction of the resulting bias is unknown, so the 31.2% describes only the subset of tweets whose accuracy two clinicians could agree on. denom_scope coded topical (health as a domain) with denom_selection curated because the corpus is a multi-issue health keyword lexicon, then randomly sub-sampled and hand-filtered. Reply tweets and retweets were removed before sampling, so the denominator is original tweets only. Saudi origin is not guaranteed: 'we cannot guarantee that all tweets had a Saudi origin.'

estimates.date: Two datasets extracted 18 May 2018 and 7 August 2018, each covering the preceding week
estimates.measure_type: % of health-related tweets from traditionally trusted health accounts classified as inaccurate
estimates.value_raw: there were 34 tweets from them and only 4 (12%) were considered inaccurate
estimates.denominator: 34 health-related tweets in the labelled set that were authored by traditionally trusted users (health professionals, health authorities and health organization accounts)
estimates.definition: Both doctors labelled the tweet inaccurate health information; author classified by two annotators from the account's self-presentation as a health professional, health authority or health organization
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, tweets are considered to be trustworthy if they are
estimates.source_quote: dataset, as there were 34 tweets from them and only 4 (12%)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-doctor accuracy coding as the main row; author type assigned by two annotators from account self-description, with five of seven disagreements resolved by discussion and two by an external expert (a surgeon with a PhD in health promotion in new media). The author classification was never externally validated.
estimates.moderator_quote: 1. Does the account holder have a health background? 2. Is the account that of an individual or nonindividual?
estimates.notes: SOURCE SUBGROUP of the main row, not an independent study estimate: these 34 tweets are a subset of the same 109. Kept because author type is a headline analytic dimension of the paper (research question 1a, Figures 5 to 7) and INSTRUCTIONS §2 lists source as a split key, but it must not be pooled alongside the 31.2% row. n = 34 is very small and the coincidence with the 34 untrustworthy tweets in the main row is accidental. Marked borderline so an adjudicator can drop it. missed_or_uncertain: Considered and not extracted: (1) '43 out of 75 (57%) of the accurate tweets were retweeted compared to 15 out of 34 (44%) of the inaccurate tweets being retweeted' — the numerator is 'was retweeted at least once' and the denominator is tweets by accuracy class, so this is a dissemination rate of misinformation, not a share of shares that are misinformation; it does not fit SHARING as defined. (2) Table 4 'Tweet accuracy: retweeted tweets (N=58) 43 (74%) accurate' — an inaccurate share among retweeted tweets would be the complement I computed, banned by R8; the paper never states it. (3) Author-composition shares that are not falsity rates: health-background individuals 'posted 29 out of 109 tweets (26.6%)'; non-health-background individuals authored '12 out of 34 (35%) of the untrustworthy tweets and only 18 out of 75 (24%) of the trustworthy tweets'; '18 out of 30 (60%) of their tweets labeled as trustworthy' (a 40% inaccurate rate for that group would be a computed complement, so not kept). (4) Feature prevalences within accuracy classes (24% of untrustworthy tweets had URLs vs 8% of trustworthy; 50% of URLs in inaccurate tweets pointed to news sites, 25% to blogs) — attributes of misinformation, not falsity shares. (5) Corpus composition (Table 1: 209,345 and 196,670 total tweets, 27.61% and 20.06% original; 552/2800 = 19.71% health-related) — topical relevance, not accuracy. (6) All figures cited from other papers, barred by R8: 4.5% of US tweets misinformed, 50% of West African tweets misinformed, Alnemer's 50% of Saudi health professionals' tweets not evidence based, 80% of governmental institutes' and 60% of physicians' tweets accurate, Kalyanam's 'almost 25% speculative', Ghenai's 39% of URLs, Wong's 70% of local health departments. (7) Figures 4 to 7 give the accuracy split by time of day and by account type only as unlabelled charts, so no values could be read from the text. rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of Arabic health tweets. Frame built from a health lexicon (100 words from three doctors plus 110 keywords from a linguistics graduate, validated against geolocated Saudi tweets); two Twitter API pulls (18 May and 7 August 2018), each limited to the preceding week, giving 209,345 and 196,670 tweets. Replies and retweets removed, leaving 97,248 original tweets; a random sample of 2,800 was drawn in Python; two non-clinical annotators filtered health relevance (60% each, 280 double-coded, Cohen kappa .872); 552 (19.71%) were health related, of which 300 were retained proportionally by dataset (180 and 120). Each of 10 forms of 30 tweets went to two doctors, who labelled accurate, inaccurate or not sure; 191 tweets were dropped for 'not sure' or disagreement, leaving 109. Author accounts classified by two annotators with discussion and one external expert. Analysis by Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon tests. Authors describe the work as a pilot and disclaim generalisability; internal validity is correlational only; Saudi origin of tweets is not guaranteed; the doctor count is reported inconsistently (10 in Methods, 20 in Limitations).
